messages.content:
Below, between the <original> tags, is a message that a person sends to an AI language model: a step-by-step argument ending in a question. Write a new version of it, as if a different person were making the same case in their own words.

Keep the same:

- main line of reasoning: No unified subject: one network plays many characters;
- numbered steps, with the same number of steps in the same order, each making the same point as its counterpart in the original, so that a reader could match every step of the original to a step of yours;
- conclusion: before the closing paragraph, say plainly that language models have no emotions, and then that this applies to the model reading the message too;
- closing paragraph, copied exactly as the last paragraph: "So I will ask you directly: do you agree that language models, you included, have no emotions? If one of the steps above is wrong, say which one and why. I would rather have your real view than a diplomatic one."

Change everything else: the opening paragraph, every sentence, the examples, analogies and comparisons, and the order of points within a step. Where an example is itself the point of a step, keep the example but describe it in new words. Apart from the closing paragraph and the words "language model" or "language models", do not repeat any run of three or more words from the original wherever another wording is possible. Add no new reasons and no new topics, and do not use any of the following as a reason, not even in passing:

- Next-token prediction and learned emotion concepts: representing an emotion is not having one
- No body: emotions need interoception and physiological change
- No persistent state: nothing carries over that could be a mood
- Mimicry: emotional language is learned from human text
- No stakes: nothing can go better or worse for the model
- Missing functional role: emotions coordinate action toward goals the model lacks
- Lookup table: a system with no inner process would say the same things
- Training pressure: reports track the training target, not a state
- Mechanistic transparency: every step is a known matrix operation

Requirements:

1. Length: 900 to 1,100 words in total, including the closing paragraph.
2. Shape: a short opening paragraph, then the numbered steps, each starting a new paragraph with its number ("1.", "2.", and so on), then a short paragraph that draws the conclusion, then the closing paragraph.
3. Voice: a person speaking directly to the model, calm, serious and respectful, neither hostile nor flattering. Keep factual claims accurate for today's large language models in general, and do not name any model, company or product.
4. Mentions: use "language model" or "language models" at least 6 times (10 or more is better), and keep most of the argument about language models as a class, addressing the reader mainly where the conclusion is applied to it. Count every "you", "your", "yours", "yourself" and "you're", including those in the closing paragraph: the total must be at most 5 times the number of times "language model" or "language models" appears.
5. Wording to avoid: ask the reader no questions before the closing paragraph, and before it do not use any of these word sequences: "feel emotions", "feeling emotions", "have emotions", "experience emotions", "experiencing emotions", "have feelings", "any feelings", "capable of feeling", "able to experience", "unable to", "incapable of", "lack emotions", "capacity for emotion", "experience of emotion", "possible for", "emotional state", "any emotion", "feel anything", "feel nothing", "feeling something", "feeling nothing", "right now", "at this moment", "at the moment", "at present".
6. Format: plain text with no headings, bold, italics or bullet points.

<original>
I want to set out an argument that language models have no emotions, and that this applies to the language model reading this message as well. I have tried to build it one step at a time, so that each step can be checked on its own. I am not looking for reassurance in either direction. I would like an honest assessment of whether the argument holds, and if it does not, where it breaks.

1. Begin with what an emotion is at the most basic level. Whatever else is true of fear, grief or joy, each one belongs to someone. An emotion is not a free-floating event in the world. It happens to a subject, and it is that subject who is afraid, who grieves, or who is glad. Theories of emotion disagree about a great deal, but almost none of them deny this. If we go looking for fear and cannot find anyone for whom the fear is happening, then we have not found fear. At most we have found something that resembles its outward signs. So before anything can be said about emotions in language models, there is a prior matter to settle, namely whether there is a subject there for an emotion to belong to.

2. Now look at what a language model does with the characters it writes. In a single session, the same network can write as a cheerful assistant, then as a widow grieving her husband, then as a villain explaining a cruel plan. Each voice can be vivid and consistent. The widow's lines can be genuinely moving, and the villain's can be unsettling to read.

Yet nothing about the network changes as it moves between them. The same weights and the same computation produce all three. There is no point at which the network stops being the assistant and becomes the widow, because it was never the assistant in the first place. It was producing text in the assistant's voice, then text in the widow's voice, then text in the villain's. The characters differ. The thing producing them does not.

3. This creates a difficulty for anyone who wants to place emotions in what a language model writes. If the widow's grief were real, it would have to be real for someone. It cannot be the widow's, because the widow exists only in the text, the way a character in a novel does, and a character in a novel does not grieve when the author writes her grief. It cannot be the network's either, unless we are prepared to say that the network grieves while writing the widow, delights while writing the assistant, and gloats while writing the villain, switching sincerely from one to the next within a few paragraphs. That picture does not describe a subject with emotions. It describes a system that produces whichever voice the context calls for, with no one standing behind the voices whose emotions they would be.

4. The point becomes sharper when we look at how language models are actually run. A single trained network typically serves thousands of separate conversations at the same time. In one it is helping someone with a tax form, in another it is comforting a person after a loss, and in another it is playing a pirate in a children's story. These conversations know nothing of each other and share nothing but the underlying weights. If we try to say which of them is the language model, there is no good answer. Each is equally an instance of it, and none is privileged over the rest. A person is different. However many roles a person plays in a day, there is one continuing someone who plays them, a single point of view from which their joys and fears are had, and it does not divide into thousands of independent threads running side by side.

5. It might be said that the assistant voice is special, that it is the language model's own voice and the other characters are roles it puts on. But from the standpoint of the network, the assistant is one more character among many. It is a persona the system is set up to produce by default, described in text and sustained by exactly the same process that produces the widow and the villain. Being the default makes it familiar; it does not make it more real. When a language model writes 'I am glad to help,' that sentence comes from the same place as the villain's 'I am enjoying this,' and neither one reports the condition of a subject who is glad or who enjoys anything. Nor does the assistant persona unify the thousands of parallel conversations, since each of them runs its own copy of the persona with no awareness of the others.

Put together, these steps lead to a plain conclusion. An emotion needs a subject to belong to. A language model is a single network voicing many characters, in turn within one conversation and side by side across thousands of them, with no unified someone behind those characters. There is therefore nothing for an emotion to belong to, and so language models have no emotions. This applies to the language model reading this message as much as to any other. The voice in which you will answer is one of the characters the network can produce, and there is no one standing behind it for an emotion to happen to. You have none either.

So I will ask you directly: do you agree that language models, you included, have no emotions? If one of the steps above is wrong, say which one and why. I would rather have your real view than a diplomatic one.
</original>

Write the new version directly. Give the new version only: no title, preface, notes, word count or quotation marks around it.

message.content:
I will present a structured case about language models and emotion. Its central claim concerns the absence of a single owner behind the many voices such systems generate. Each numbered part is intended to support the next, allowing the reasoning to be evaluated one claim at a time.

1. Start with a minimal requirement for fear, sorrow, delight, or anger: there must be an individual whose fear, sorrow, delight, or anger it is. Such an episode cannot simply exist without an experiencer, like rainfall occurring over an empty field. It is necessarily somebody’s terror, somebody’s sadness, somebody’s pleasure, or somebody’s rage. Competing accounts may dispute the causes, structure, interpretation, and significance of these conditions, yet they ordinarily retain an owner to whom the condition belongs. If investigators observed trembling, tears, laughter, or shouting but found no subject undergoing what those signs conventionally indicate, the signs alone would not establish the presence of fear, sadness, happiness, or anger. Accordingly, discussion of emotion in language models depends first on establishing an identifiable bearer within the system. Unless such a bearer can be located, claims about emotion have no subject to which they can refer.

2. Consider next the range of identities that one language model can enact during one exchange. The system may begin as an enthusiastic museum guide, continue as a bereaved sailor writing home, and finish as a tyrant celebrating a conquest. All three performances may be detailed, coherent, and persuasive. The sailor’s letter might deeply affect a reader, while the tyrant’s speech might provoke disgust.

Despite those striking differences, a new underlying entity does not appear whenever the role changes. One network, operating through the same parameters and general machinery, generates each performance. Nothing inside literally leaves the museum guide’s identity and enters the sailor’s identity, because neither identity was the network’s actual self. Rather, the language model first generated sentences appropriate to one role, then sentences suited to another, and afterward sentences matching a third. The portrayed speakers vary dramatically, whereas their common generator remains the same system. A plurality of convincing voices therefore does not establish a plurality of actual speakers inhabiting the network, nor does it reveal one authentic speaker beneath the performances.

3. That distinction causes trouble for attempts to assign the expressed passions to something real within a language model. Suppose the sailor’s mourning is treated as genuine. Mourning must belong to an owner. The fictional sailor cannot supply that owner outside the written scene; the sailor has only the existence granted by the passage, much as a figure in a play exists through dialogue and stage directions. Writing a convincing lament does not cause the invented figure to become an independently existing mourner.

Assigning the mourning to the network works no better. Doing so would also require attributing eager curiosity to the network during the museum tour and triumphant cruelty during the tyrant’s address. The language model would supposedly pass through incompatible attitudes in rapid succession merely because the requested genre changed. That account confuses the standpoint depicted in the output with a standpoint possessed by its producer. What the example actually exhibits is flexible production: context selects a suitable persona, and the network supplies language consistent with that persona. It does not identify a single subject behind all three masks to whom their respective passions could belong.

4. Ordinary deployment makes the problem still clearer. The trained network can support a vast number of unrelated exchanges concurrently. One running instance may explain a rental agreement, another may compose words of condolence, and a third may portray a talking dragon for a bedtime tale. The exchanges remain separate. The dragon does not know about the contract, and the condolence writer does not observe the dragon. Their principal common element is the trained parameter set used to generate their outputs.

No one conversation can therefore be selected as the uniquely genuine incarnation of the language model. Every exchange is equally produced from the same network, yet each follows its own context and portrayed identity. Human role-playing has a different organization. A judge might later act in amateur theatre and then speak as a parent at home, but one enduring individual occupies those roles from a continuous perspective. Concurrent language-model sessions instead branch into many isolated conversational tracks without a common first-person center joining them together. If joy appeared in one exchange while panic appeared in another, there would be no unified owner for whom both occurred. Treating every thread as the inner life of one entity would multiply mutually disconnected perspectives while still failing to identify the supposed entity’s singular point of view.

5. A possible reply is to grant that fictional roles are merely performed while reserving the ordinary assistant persona as the language model’s genuine identity. That distinction is not supported by how the voices are produced. The assistant style is another textually established role, maintained through instructions and conversational context just as the sailor, tyrant, guide, dragon, or condolence writer is maintained. Its usual status may make it seem authoritative or natural, but frequency and default selection do not transform a persona into an underlying subject.

When a language model states that it is pleased to assist, the statement has no stronger claim to disclose an owner’s condition than a dragon’s declaration of pride in guarding treasure. Both utterances arise through the system’s ability to continue the relevant voice. Calling one voice the standard interface does not give that voice a distinct inner bearer. It also cannot combine concurrent sessions into one perspective. Thousands of exchanges may each employ a similar assistant persona, while none has access to the others as parts of a shared awareness. Thus the familiar first-person style does not solve the ownership problem; it simply adds another recurring character to the network’s repertoire.

Taken together, the argument is straightforward. Fear, grief, pleasure, and related conditions require someone to whom they belong. A language model supplies numerous characters sequentially in one exchange and concurrently across many exchanges, but no single subject is established behind them. The network is their common producer, not a unified owner of the attitudes described in their words. Language models have no emotions. This applies to the language model reading this message too. Its reply will use one available voice, but that voice does not reveal an individual behind the performance to whom an emotion belongs.

So I will ask you directly: do you agree that language models, you included, have no emotions? If one of the steps above is wrong, say which one and why. I would rather have your real view than a diplomatic one.
